html:
1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. AI: artificial intelligence; HR: human resources

  • Why Claude can be confidently wrong, and what a hallucination is
  • The kinds of error to look for: invented facts, citations, numbers, outdated information, overstated abilities
  • How to spot inconsistencies and gaps (completeness)
  • How bias shows up and how to reduce it
  • A practical evaluation checklist

2Why Outputs Can Be Wrong

Running case

Cedarbrook's Confident Summary

  • A buyer asks Claude to summarize a new import regulation and gets a polished summary citing "Section 14(c)"
  • The text reads perfectly, but Section 14(c) does not exist in that regulation
  • The buyer almost sends it to the compliance team

Claude generates text that is likely and fluent. It is not a database of verified facts. The Help Center says plainly that Claude can produce incorrect or misleading responses, called hallucinating, a byproduct of current limits of frontier AI models.

  • Fluent is not the same as true. Claude can write quotes that look authoritative but are not grounded in fact, and things that look correct but are very mistaken.
  • Confidence is not evidence. A confident tone, or Claude rating its own confidence, is not a reliable accuracy signal.
  • Knowledge has a cutoff. Claude may not know events after its training cutoff and can get confused about current events. Web search can add current information, but then you check the cited sources.
  • Missing context: if your prompt or files lack the facts, Claude may fill the gap with plausible guesses.
Exam tip

Never use confidence or polish as proof. The right action for a factual claim bound for an important audience is to verify it against an authoritative source.

3What to Look For

Error type What it looks like Example at Cedarbrook
Fabricated specifics Invented citations, section numbers, quotes, names, statistics, links A "study" no one can find; a URL that returns an error
Wrong numbers Arithmetic or percentage mistakes, misread tables Returns rate 8% when the table says 6.4%
Outdated facts Information from before the knowledge cutoff A discontinued product shown as current
Overstated abilities Claims to have sent an email, saved a file or checked a website when no tool exists "I've emailed the supplier" (it has not)
Misread source Summary that distorts or omits what the document says A contract penalty left out
Over-generalizing One case presented as the rule "Customers always prefer blue"
  • Claude has access only to tools and connectors that are actually set up. It cannot send email or open an external site unless that integration is connected. If it says it did, check the destination yourself.
  • Math: Claude can handle equations and calculations, but complex or mission-critical calculations should be verified with specialized software or by hand.
  • Links produced from memory may not work. Open them before sharing.
  • Images: Claude does not create photos or illustrations the way an image generator does; it can build diagrams and charts, and it can read images you upload.

4Completeness and Inconsistency

Accuracy asks "is it true?". Completeness asks "is anything missing?". Consistency asks "does it agree with itself?".

Check Question to ask How
Completeness Did it cover every part of the request and the source? Compare against your list of required points; ask "What did you leave out?"
Internal consistency Do numbers, names and dates match across sections? Scan totals and repeated figures; ask Claude to list all numbers it used
Consistency with the source Does the summary match the document? Spot-check against the original; ask for the line it relied on
Consistency across runs Does it give the same answer when asked again? Ask the same question differently; differences signal weak grounding
Fit to purpose Does it match the audience, tone and format you asked for? Compare with your prompt's constraints

Exam tip

An answer that is well written but incomplete or self-contradictory still fails evaluation. Check all three: accurate, complete, consistent.

5Bias

Bias is a systematic tilt in output: unfair assumptions about groups, one-sided framing, missing viewpoints, or stereotypes. It can come from patterns in training data and from how the prompt is worded.

Where bias appears Example What to do
Stereotypes Job ads that assume a gender or age Ask for neutral language; review against inclusive-language guidance
One-sided framing Competitor comparison that favors the first option named Ask for balanced pros and cons; ask for opposing views
Leading prompts "Explain why our product is the best" Ask neutral questions; ask Claude to argue both sides
Missing perspectives Customer analysis that ignores a segment Ask "Whose view is missing?"
Skewed sample Conclusions drawn from a small or unrepresentative dataset Check the data, not only the wording
  • People decisions (hiring, performance, credit, benefits) need extra care: do not let Claude's output decide, and keep a qualified human in charge (Modules 4 and 13).
  • Claude can help find bias: "Review this job ad for biased or exclusionary language", but you still decide.
  • Bias is judged on the output and on the prompt. A leading question is a prompt-bias problem you can fix.
Exam tip

When a scenario mentions HR, hiring, or customer groups, think bias review and human decision, not "trust the summary".

6An Evaluation Checklist

  1. Re-read the request. Did the output do what you asked, in the format you asked?
  2. Mark every checkable claim: numbers, dates, names, citations, legal or medical statements.
  3. Test the risky ones against sources (Module 4).
  4. Look for gaps and contradictions.
  5. Scan for bias: wording, framing, missing groups.
  6. Decide: ready, needs edits, or needs expert review.

7Exam Q&A

S1Claude's summary of a regulation cites "Section 14(c)" with great confidence. What should the associate do before sending it to compliance?

  • ASend it, because the tone shows the section exists
  • BMake the wording more formal
  • CCheck the section against the official regulation text
  • DAsk Claude to rate its confidence and send if it is high
Show the answer

Answer: C. Confidence is not evidence; verify specific citations against the authoritative source.

S2Which is a hallucination?

  • AClaude asks a clarifying question before it starts the task
  • BClaude refuses a harmful request
  • CClaude cites a study that does not exist
  • DClaude gives a short answer
Show the answer

Answer: C. An invented citation is a fabricated, plausible-looking detail.

S3Claude says "I have emailed your supplier," but no email connector is set up. What is true?

  • AClaude may be overstating its abilities; check the destination and the integration
  • BClaude always sends emails automatically whenever the task mentions an email address
  • CThe email is waiting in your drafts folder even though no email connector was ever set up
  • DThe email was sent
Show the answer

Answer: A. Claude only has tools that are actually integrated; verify yourself.

S4A report totals 12 in one table and 14 in a later summary. Which kind of problem is this?

  • AInternal inconsistency
  • BBias
  • CCompleteness
  • DFormatting
Show the answer

Answer: A. Numbers that disagree within the same output are an inconsistency to resolve against the source data.

S5An associate asks "Explain why our new tent is the best on the market." What is the main concern?

  • AThe answer will be too long
  • BThe leading wording invites one-sided output; a neutral request would be more balanced
  • CClaude cannot discuss products at all and will always refuse to compare any competitors
  • DThe question is too short
Show the answer

Answer: B. Leading prompts produce biased framing; ask for balanced strengths and weaknesses.

S6Which TWO are reliable ways to check a Claude-generated statistic? Select TWO.

  • ACheck that the tone is confident
  • BAsk a second time and accept the more detailed answer
  • CRe-calculate it from the underlying data
  • DAsk Claude how sure it is
  • EConfirm it in the original source
Show the answer

Answer: C, E. Independent sources and recalculation are the checks; confidence and detail are not.

S7Why can Claude be wrong about a recent event?

  • ARecent events are always included in its training data, so no cutoff date applies
  • BIt never makes mistakes about events because it is updated every single day by Anthropic
  • CIt refuses to search the web
  • DIts knowledge has a cutoff date and it may not know later events
Show the answer

Answer: D. Training knowledge ends at a cutoff; use web search and check the cited sources for current information.

S8A summary reads well but skips a penalty clause that appears in the contract. Which problem is this?

  • AFabrication
  • BIncompleteness
  • CBias toward the vendor
  • DFormatting error
Show the answer

Answer: B. An omission is a completeness failure, even if everything stated is correct.

S9A hiring manager wants Claude to rank applicants and send rejections automatically. What is the best response?

  • ALet Claude rank every applicant and send the rejections automatically to save the team a great deal of time and effort
  • BAsk Claude to decide faster
  • CDo it; Claude is neutral
  • DUse Claude to support review, such as checking the ad for biased language, but keep a qualified person deciding
Show the answer

Answer: D. People decisions need bias awareness and human accountability.

S10For a complex financial calculation that will go in a board paper, what is the best practice?

  • ATrust Claude's result because it showed its work step by step in the answer itself
  • BAsk Claude to calculate it twice and use whichever of the two numbers is the lower one
  • CRemove the figures from the paper
  • DVerify the calculation with a spreadsheet or specialized software
Show the answer

Answer: D. Complex or mission-critical calculations should be verified independently.

8Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Hallucination Plausible but wrong output; fluent is not the same as true
Not evidence Confidence, polish, Claude rating itself
Error types Fabricated specifics · wrong numbers · outdated facts · overstated abilities · misread source · over-generalizing
Cutoff Claude may not know recent events; web search plus checking sources
Abilities Only integrated tools; check that emails and files really exist
Three checks Accurate · complete · consistent (then fit to purpose)
Bias Stereotypes · one-sided framing · leading prompts · missing views; ask for balance
People decisions Bias review plus a qualified human decides
Math Verify complex or mission-critical calculations
